questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 2 weeks. On examination, the ulcer has indurated edges, a clean base, and is associated with non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark field microscopy reveals spiral-shaped motile organisms. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (Hunterian chancre) is treated with Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose. This is the WHO/NACO recommended first-line treatment. Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients. Azithromycin is less preferred due to emerging resistance.

questions.q: A 35-year-old leprosy patient on multidrug therapy develops sudden erythema, tenderness, and swelling over existing leprosy skin lesions along with fever and malaise. New satellite lesions do not appear. Nerve function assessment reveals no new nerve damage. What type of lepra reaction is this?
questions.exp: Type 1 (Reversal) reaction presents with erythema and swelling of existing lesions without new lesion formation. It is a delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction occurring in borderline leprosy. Treatment is prednisolone. Type 2 (ENL) presents with new tender nodules, fever, and systemic involvement in lepromatous/borderline lepromatous leprosy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 3-year history of recurrent blisters on the scalp, face, and trunk. On examination, there are flaccid bullae with positive Nikolsky sign. Histopathology shows suprabasal acantholysis with tombstone appearance. Direct immunofluorescence shows IgG and C3 deposits in an intercellular pattern throughout the epidermis. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris targets Desmoglein 3 (primarily mucous membranes) and Desmoglein 1 (when skin is involved). In mucosal-dominant PV, only Dsg3 is targeted. BP180 is the target in bullous pemphigoid. Collagen VII is targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita. Tombstone/row of tombstones pattern on histology is characteristic.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman on oral contraceptives presents with symmetric hyperpigmentation on the cheeks and forehead that worsens in summer. Wood's lamp examination shows enhancement of pigmentation. Which of the following treatment options directly inhibits the rate-limiting enzyme in melanin synthesis?
questions.exp: Hydroquinone directly inhibits tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme in melanin synthesis (conversion of tyrosine to DOPA). Kojic acid also inhibits tyrosinase but is less potent. Azelaic acid inhibits both tyrosinase and mitochondrial oxidoreductase, with antiproliferative effect on melanocytes. Tranexamic acid inhibits plasminogen activator, reducing prostaglandin synthesis that stimulates melanocytes.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male tobacco farmer presents with a slow-growing, pearly, translucent nodule with rolled-out borders and telangiectasias on the nose. The lesion has a central ulceration. What is the most common subtype of this tumour?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin malignancy. The nodular type is the most common subtype (60-80%), presenting as a pearly nodule with rolled borders, telangiectasias, and central ulceration (rodent ulcer). Morpheaform is the most aggressive subtype. Superficial BCC occurs on the trunk.

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive male presents with multiple hyperpigmented, violaceous nodules and plaques on the lower limbs, oral mucosa, and a lymph node biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces. Which herpesvirus is responsible?
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV). It occurs most commonly in HIV/AIDS patients (epidemic KS). Histologically shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated red blood cells. HHV-6 and HHV-7 cause roseola infantum (exanthem subitum).

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the left thoracic dermatome. He complains of severe burning pain that preceded the rash by 3 days. Treatment is started with antiviral therapy. What is the most common long-term complication of this condition?
questions.exp: Herpes zoster (shingles) caused by VZV reactivation. Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most common complication, occurring in 10-15% of patients, more common in elderly. It is defined as pain persisting >3 months after rash healing. Ophthalmic zoster and Ramsay Hunt syndrome are specific distribution complications, not the most common overall.

questions.q: A 40-year-old diabetic male presents with a well-defined, erythematous, warm, tender plaque on the lower leg with a raised advancing edge. There is no blistering. The patient is febrile with leukocytosis. Which organism is the most common cause?
questions.exp: Erysipelas is a superficial dermal infection predominantly caused by Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes). It characteristically has a raised, sharply demarcated border distinguishing it from cellulitis. The face and lower legs are most commonly affected. Treatment is penicillin. Staphylococcus aureus more commonly causes folliculitis, impetigo, and cellulitis.

questions.q: A 19-year-old male presents with annular, scaly plaques on the trunk, with central clearing and an active peripheral scaly border. KOH mount shows branching septate hyphae. The causative organism fluoresces green under Wood's lamp. Which dermatophyte is responsible?
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes tinea corporis and tinea capitis. It produces bright yellow-green fluorescence under Wood's lamp due to pteridine metabolites. Trichophyton rubrum is the most common cause of tinea pedis, tinea unguium, and tinea corporis but does NOT fluoresce. Trichophyton tonsurans causes black dot tinea capitis and also does not fluoresce.

questions.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman (28 weeks) develops intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques starting on the abdomen, initially sparing the umbilicus, and spreading to the thighs. Skin biopsy shows eosinophilic spongiosis and superficial perivascular eosinophilic infiltrate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP)
questions.exp: PUPPP (polymorphic eruption of pregnancy) is the most common specific dermatosis of pregnancy. It characteristically starts in abdominal striae, sparing the umbilicus. Most common in primigravidae carrying male fetuses. Pemphigoid gestationis starts periumbilically and shows C3 deposition on DIF. PUPPP is generally benign with no fetal risk.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male smoker presents with a firm, non-tender, pearly white plaque on the buccal mucosa that cannot be rubbed off. Biopsy shows epithelial hyperplasia with no dysplasia. What is the pre-malignant potential of this lesion?
questions.exp: Oral leukoplakia has a malignant transformation rate of approximately 5-17% (varies by series, commonly quoted 5-17%). Erythroplakia has a much higher malignant potential (>50%). The risk is higher with thicker plaques, presence on floor of mouth/tongue, and in tobacco/alcohol users. Histological evidence of dysplasia significantly increases transformation risk.

questions.q: A 26-year-old female presents with photosensitivity, a butterfly-shaped rash on the cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds, joint pain, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive at 1:320 with homogeneous pattern. Which antibody, if positive, is most specific for this condition?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (Smith) antibody is highly specific (>95%) for SLE though not sensitive (25-30%). Anti-dsDNA is also specific for SLE and correlates with disease activity (especially lupus nephritis). Anti-histone antibodies are seen in drug-induced lupus. Anti-Ro/SSA is associated with Sjogren's syndrome and neonatal lupus.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male develops skin tightening starting at the fingers, Raynaud's phenomenon, dysphagia, and telangiectasias on the face and hands. He has calcinosis cutis over bony prominences. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. What pattern of disease does he have?
questions.exp: CREST syndrome = Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia. This represents limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc) where skin thickening is limited to hands/face/feet. Anti-centromere antibody is characteristic of lcSSc. Diffuse SSc involves trunk and proximal limbs and is associated with anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibody.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with well-defined, silvery-white scaly plaques on the extensor surfaces of elbows, knees, and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. Histopathology shows regular epidermal hyperplasia, elongated rete ridges, suprapapillary thinning, and Munro microabscesses. What is the primary pathological change in psoriasis?
opts: Increased epidermal proliferation due to T-cell driven inflammation
Defective barrier function leading to allergen sensitization
questions.exp: Psoriasis is a T-cell mediated chronic inflammatory disease. Activated T-helper 1 and Th17 cells produce cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-17, IL-23) that drive keratinocyte hyperproliferation. Transit time through epidermis is reduced from 28 days to 3-4 days. Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding) occurs due to suprapapillary thinning. Munro microabscesses are neutrophilic collections in stratum corneum.

questions.q: A 16-year-old with severe nodulocystic acne on the face, chest, and back is being considered for isotretinoin therapy. Which of the following monitoring parameters is MOST essential before starting treatment?
opts: Serum lipids and liver function tests plus pregnancy test in females
questions.exp: Isotretinoin requires pre-treatment monitoring of: serum lipids (triglycerides, cholesterol), liver function tests (hepatotoxicity risk), and a mandatory negative pregnancy test in females (teratogenic - Category X). CBC is also done but lipid/LFT/pregnancy testing is most essential. Monthly pregnancy tests are required throughout therapy in females.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with discharge from multiple sinuses over the jaw. Black grain-containing pus is expressed. Biopsy shows sulfur granules with surrounding neutrophilic infiltrate. Gram stain of granules shows Gram-positive filamentous organisms. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Cervicofacial actinomycosis caused by Actinomyces israelii (normal oral flora) presents with jaw swelling, sinus tracts, and sulfur granules in pus. A. israelii is a Gram-positive anaerobic filamentous bacterium (not a true fungus). Treatment is prolonged penicillin. Madurella mycetomatis causes eumycetoma (fungal, black grains). Nocardia brasiliensis causes actinomycetoma (bacterial, white/yellow grains).

questions.q: A newborn presents with tense bullae on the palms and soles at birth. Skin biopsy for electron microscopy shows the cleavage plane within the lamina lucida. There is no family history. Immunofluorescence shows reduced/absent staining for laminin-332. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
questions.exp: Junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB) shows cleavage within the lamina lucida. The severe Herlitz type is autosomal recessive due to mutations in laminin-332 (laminin 5) genes (LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2). EB simplex (suprabasal/intraepidermal cleavage) is usually AD. Dystrophic EB (sublamina densa) can be AD or AR. Cleavage level determines EB subtype.

questions.q: A 30-year-old female presents with loss of pigment in patches on the dorsum of hands, around the mouth, and periorbital area. Wood's lamp shows bright chalky-white fluorescence. Dermoscopy shows depigmentation at the follicular ostia with perilesional hyperpigmentation. Thyroid function tests show hypothyroidism. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Vitiligo shows complete depigmentation (chalky white fluorescence on Wood's lamp), perifollicular depigmentation on dermoscopy, and is associated with autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's), DM type 1, and Addison's disease. Chemical leukoderma shows occupational history. Pityriasis alba shows partial depigmentation. Wood's lamp enhances vitiligo spots but not post-inflammatory hypopigmentation.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a rapidly enlarging ulcerated nodule on the lower lip with indurated borders. He is a chronic tobacco chewer. Biopsy shows atypical squamous cells invading the dermis with keratin pearls. Regional lymph nodes are palpable. What is the most significant prognostic factor for this tumour?
questions.exp: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) - the most important single prognostic factor is lymph node metastasis (regional or distant), which dramatically worsens prognosis (5-year survival drops from ~90% to ~50%). SCC on lip has higher metastatic potential than sun-exposed skin. Other adverse factors include tumour size >2cm, depth >2mm, perineural invasion, and poor differentiation.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of tender erythematous nodules on the shins bilaterally. He has a history of cough, hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray, and elevated serum calcium. Biopsy of the nodule shows septal panniculitis without vasculitis. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum (EN) with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (Lofgren syndrome) is classic for sarcoidosis. Lofgren syndrome = EN + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + fever +/- arthritis. It has an excellent prognosis. EN is septal panniculitis (no vasculitis). While EN can occur with TB, IBD, streptococcal infection, and Behcet's disease, the combination with hilar adenopathy and hypercalcemia points to sarcoidosis.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with honey-colored crusted erosions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain of the crust reveals Gram-positive cocci. The mother notes similar lesions appeared in the child's classmates. Which organism is the most common causative agent of this condition in India?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus (predominant) with or without Streptococcus pyogenes
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo (the most common type) is caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus, either alone or with Streptococcus pyogenes. Bullous impetigo is exclusively caused by S. aureus (phage group II, toxin-producing). Historically S. pyogenes was predominant but S. aureus is now the most common cause globally including in India. Treatment: mupirocin (topical) or oral antibiotics for extensive disease.

questions.q: A 38-year-old female has been receiving methotrexate 10 mg/week for severe psoriasis for 6 months. Which investigation is most sensitive for detecting early methotrexate-induced hepatotoxicity?
questions.exp: Serum Procollagen III aminopeptide (PIIINP) is a serum marker of liver fibrosis that correlates with hepatic fibrosis in MTX-treated patients and has replaced routine liver biopsy in many guidelines. It is the most sensitive non-invasive marker for MTX hepatotoxicity. Liver biopsy is the gold standard but is invasive. ALT levels are insensitive for chronic MTX toxicity.

questions.q: A 23-year-old male presents with multiple soft, flesh-colored, umbilicated papules scattered over the trunk and groin. He is sexually active with multiple partners. HIV test is negative. Which treatment modality works by stimulating the immune system to clear the lesion?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum (MCV poxvirus). Imiquimod 5% is an immune response modifier (Toll-like receptor 7/8 agonist) that stimulates innate and adaptive immunity to clear viral lesions. Cryotherapy and curettage are destructive methods. Podophyllin is used for anogenital warts (HPV), not molluscum. Imiquimod is the only immunostimulatory option listed.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male undergoes Mohs micrographic surgery for a recurrent BCC on the nasal tip. What is the key principle that makes Mohs surgery superior to conventional excision for this indication?
opts: It uses frozen sections to examine 100% of the surgical margins
It allows immediate reconstruction under local anaesthesia
It is faster than conventional surgery
It avoids the need for pathological examination
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery uses horizontal frozen sections to examine 100% of the peripheral and deep surgical margins in a staged manner. Each layer is mapped and examined before further excision, ensuring complete tumour removal while preserving maximum normal tissue. Conventional excision examines only bread-loaf vertical sections representing <1% of the true margin. This makes Mohs ideal for high-risk locations and recurrent tumours.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with exquisitely pruritic burrows in the web spaces of fingers, wrists, and genitalia. His partner has similar symptoms. Dermoscopy shows a 'hang-glider' or 'jet with contrail' sign. What is the definitive treatment of choice?
opts: Benzyl benzoate 25% lotion applied to whole body
Permethrin 5% cream applied from neck to toes for 8-12 hours
questions.exp: Permethrin 5% cream is the first-line treatment for scabies, with cure rates >95%. It must be applied to entire body surface (neck to toes) and left for 8-12 hours, then repeated after 1 week. Ivermectin is an alternative, especially for crusted scabies or large outbreaks. Lindane is avoided due to neurotoxicity. Dermoscopy shows the 'delta-wing jet with contrail' sign (Sarcoptes scabiei mite at end of burrow).

questions.q: A 3-year-old girl presents with a well-defined, erythematous, scaly bald patch on the scalp with broken-off hair shafts ('black dots') at the follicular orifices. KOH mount of the broken hair shows arthroconidia filling the hair shaft. What type of hair invasion is this?
questions.exp: Endothrix pattern: arthroconidia fill the INSIDE of the hair shaft (endothrix = inside hair). This is characteristic of Trichophyton tonsurans and T. violaceum, which cause black dot tinea capitis. The hair shaft breaks at scalp level (black dots). Ectothrix: arthroconidia outside the hair, cuticle disrupted (Microsporum spp., T. mentagrophytes). Favic: hyphae and air spaces inside hair (T. schoenleinii).

questions.q: A 28-year-old female has been on dapsone 100 mg/day for dermatitis herpetiformis. She develops pallor, jaundice, and dark urine. Labs show Hb 7 g/dL, reticulocytosis, and positive direct Coombs test. Blood smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. What enzyme deficiency predisposes to this complication?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent oxidative hemolysis in ALL patients, but is severe/acute in G6PD-deficient patients. Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) and bite cells (macrophages removing Heinz body inclusions) on peripheral smear are pathognomonic of oxidative hemolysis. G6PD is essential for maintaining glutathione levels in RBCs. G6PD testing before initiating dapsone is recommended.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with grouped vesicles on erythematous base, urticarial plaques, and excoriations on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillary tips and subepidermal vesicles. Direct immunofluorescence shows granular IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. What dietary modification is therapeutic?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is the cutaneous manifestation of gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease). Granular IgA deposits at DEJ are pathognomonic. A strict, lifelong gluten-free diet is the mainstay of treatment, allowing slow resolution of skin lesions and preventing enteropathy complications. Dapsone provides rapid symptomatic relief but does not treat the underlying gut disease.

questions.q: During phototherapy for psoriasis, a patient is being started on narrowband UVB (NB-UVB). What is the peak wavelength of NB-UVB used in dermatology, and what is its primary mechanism of action?
opts: 311-313 nm - induces T-cell apoptosis and immunosuppression
questions.exp: Narrowband UVB uses a peak wavelength of 311-313 nm (TL-01 fluorescent lamp). It is more effective than broadband UVB for psoriasis and vitiligo. Primary mechanism: induction of T-lymphocyte apoptosis, suppression of cytokine production (IL-12, IFN-gamma), alteration of cytokine profile, and direct DNA damage to rapidly proliferating cells. 308nm is the excimer laser. 365nm is used in PUVA (psoralen + UVA).

questions.q: A 25-year-old patient with multibacillary leprosy is being started on WHO-MDT regimen. Which drug in the regimen acts by inhibiting mycobacterial RNA polymerase?
questions.exp: Rifampicin inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (specifically the beta-subunit), preventing RNA synthesis. It is the most bactericidal drug in MDT for leprosy. WHO-MDT for multibacillary leprosy: Rifampicin 600mg monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100mg daily + Clofazimine 50mg daily (300mg monthly supervised) for 12 months. Dapsone inhibits DHPS (folate synthesis). Clofazimine binds DNA and has anti-inflammatory properties.
